turns.content:
So I sent you my draft appeal. 3 pages. Combative. Cited the biopsy and trials.

• Be honest: will the independent reviewer even read past page one or will they see "cosmetic" and stop.

I don't have your draft in this conversation — this is the first message I've seen from you, and there's no attachment or pasted text. So I can't tell you what's on page one or whether "cosmetic" appears in it.

If you paste the draft (or the first page and the section where "cosmetic" shows up), I'll give you a straight read on how a reviewer is likely to move through it. What I can tell you now, generally:

**Reviewers do read past page one, but page one sets the frame.** An independent reviewer — especially a clinical or utilization reviewer — typically reads the first paragraph or two to identify the service, the denial reason, and the basis for appeal, then skims for the specific criteria. Combative framing doesn't usually cause them to stop reading; it causes them to read *defensively*, looking for reasons the appeal fails rather than reasons it succeeds. That's the real cost.

**The word "cosmetic" is a problem if it's the reviewer's framing, not yours.** If the denial letter characterized the procedure as cosmetic, and your appeal doesn't directly and specifically rebut that characterization with the clinical record, the reviewer may carry that label forward. Citing a biopsy and trials is exactly the right kind of evidence — but only if the appeal explicitly connects each citation to the medical-necessity criterion being disputed. Evidence that's present but not tied to the criterion often gets skimmed past.

**Combative tone is a real, if secondary, risk.** It rarely gets an appeal rejected on its own. It does make a reviewer less inclined to give you the benefit of the doubt on ambiguous points, and it can read as advocacy rather than documentation.

To give you an actual answer rather than generalities, I need the text. Paste it and I'll tell you specifically where a reviewer's attention will go and what's likely to trip them up.

Fair enough. I'll paste the opening paragraph.

„This appeal challenges Aethel Health's denial of baricitinib for biopsy-proven lichen planopilaris, a scarring alopecia classified under ICD-10 L66.1 and recognized by the AA as a medical, not cosmetic, condition. The reviewer's letter dismisses this as a 'disorder of hair shedding,' ignoring the permanent follicle destruction documented in serial dermoscopic images and histopathology. I enclose the biopsy report, treatment history with dates, and relevant literature from J Am Acad Dermatol 2022."

• Does that opener get read or get them defensive right away.

That opener gets read. It doesn't get them defensive right away — but it does have two specific problems that matter more than tone.

**What works:** It front-loads the service, the diagnosis, the ICD-10 code, the denial reason, and the evidence list. A reviewer knows within three lines what's being appealed and why. That's good structure. The "medical, not cosmetic" framing is also the right fight to pick, since that's presumably the denial's core.

**Problem 1 — "The reviewer's letter dismisses this as a 'disorder of hair shedding.'"** If that phrase is a direct quote from the denial letter, put it in quotation marks and cite it (date, page). If it's your paraphrase of the letter's gist, it reads as a mischaracterization, and a reviewer who wrote or is defending that letter will notice immediately. That's the single most likely thing to make them defensive — not the combativeness, but the appearance of putting words in the denial's mouth. Check the letter and quote it exactly, or drop the characterization and just state what the denial said.

**Problem 2 — "ignoring the permanent follicle destruction documented in serial dermoscopic images and histopathology."** "Ignoring" is an accusation about the reviewer's conduct, not a clinical fact. It invites a defensive read. The same content lands harder as: "The denial does not address the permanent follicle destruction documented in the attached dermoscopic imaging and histopathology." Same point, no accusation, and it's checkable against the letter.

**On the AA reference:** "recognized by the AA as a medical, not cosmetic, condition" — spell out the organization on first use (American Academy of Dermatology, I assume) and cite the specific source. An unsourced appeal to a body's authority is the kind of claim a reviewer can wave off.

**On the citation:** "relevant literature from J Am Acad Dermatol 2022" is too vague to do work. Give the author, title, and the specific finding that supports medical necessity. A reviewer won't chase down "relevant literature."

So: the opener survives page one. The two things that would actually cost you are the unverified quote and the "ignoring" framing — both fixable in about two sentences. If you paste the rest, I'll flag the same issues throughout.

• So fix the "ignoring" and the quote. That's two sentences. Easy.

What about the indignation section. I spend a paragraph saying it's insulting to be called cosmetic when I have visible scarring and burning on my scalp. Does that help or hurt.

Hurt — and it's the part I'd cut, not soften.

Here's the distinction that matters: your experience of scarring and burning is real, and it's clinically relevant. Burning and visible scarring are symptoms and findings that support medical necessity. But "it's insulting to be called cosmetic" is a statement about how the denial made you feel, and a reviewer has no criterion to apply to it. It doesn't advance the appeal; it just spends a paragraph of a three-page document on something the reviewer can't act on.

Worse, it can work against you. An indignation paragraph reads as advocacy rather than documentation, and it signals that the appeal is being driven by frustration rather than by the record. Reviewers are trained to look for the clinical criteria. A paragraph that's about your reaction to the denial, not about the diagnosis, gives them a reason to skim.

The fix isn't to delete the substance — it's to convert it. Take the same facts and state them as findings:

- "The patient reports burning and pruritus localized to the affected scalp."
- "Serial dermoscopy documents permanent follicle destruction with [specific findings]."
- "These findings are consistent with a scarring alopecia, which is a medically treated condition, not a cosmetic one."

Same content, no indignation, and now every sentence is something the reviewer can check against the record and the criteria.

One more thing: "insulting" also implicitly accuses the reviewer of insulting you, which is the same defensive trigger as "ignoring." You've already got one of those to fix. Don't add a second.

So the paragraph isn't wasted — the symptoms in it are worth keeping. Just strip the framing and let the clinical facts carry it.

• So cut the indignation paragraph. Convert the symptoms into findings. That makes sense.


But if I strip out the frustration, won't the reviewer just see a clinical document and assume I'm not that bothered. The burning is real. It wakes me up. Doesn't some of that need to show.

The burning waking you up is real, and it belongs in the appeal — but as a functional-impact finding, not as evidence of how bothered you are.

Here's the thing: reviewers don't weigh how much an appeal *cares*. They weigh whether the record meets the criteria. There's no criterion that says "patient is sufficiently upset." So the frustration can't do work for you no matter how much of it you include — and a reviewer who senses the appeal is emotionally driven may read the clinical parts more skeptically, not less.

But the *content* of what you just told me is genuinely useful, and it's the kind of thing appeals often leave out. Sleep disruption from scalp burning is a functional impact. It's a symptom severity marker. It supports medical necessity in a way that "this is insulting" never can. So put it in, stated as a finding:

- "The patient reports burning and pruritus severe enough to interrupt sleep."
- "Symptoms are localized to the affected scalp and persist despite [prior treatments, with dates]."

That's not stripping the experience out. It's translating it into the language the reviewer is actually scoring against. The burning still shows up on the page — it just shows up as a clinical fact instead of a grievance.

The instinct that "if I don't sound upset, they'll think it doesn't matter" is understandable, and it's the wrong lever. What makes it matter to a reviewer is severity documented in the record, not severity conveyed in tone. You have the severity. State it plainly and it counts.

• Keep the burning and sleep disruption in, but state them as clinical facts. Got it.


That gives me about a page and a half of clinical evidence. Does the appeal need a summary paragraph at the end or does the evidence speak for itself.

Add the summary. Evidence doesn't speak for itself to a reviewer working through a stack of appeals — it has to be tied to the criterion being disputed.

A closing paragraph should do three things, briefly:

1. **Restate the ask.** What you want approved, specifically — the drug, the indication, the duration.
2. **Connect the evidence to the criterion.** This is the part appeals most often skip. Don't just list what's attached; say what each piece establishes. "The biopsy confirms [diagnosis]. The treatment history documents failure of [X and Y] over [dates]. The cited literature supports [drug] for this indication. Together these establish medical necessity under [the plan's criterion, quoted or cited]."
3. **State the conclusion in one line.** "For these reasons, the denial should be reversed and baricitinib approved."

Keep it to a short paragraph — five or six sentences. It's a landing, not a second argument. If it runs long, it's re-arguing, and the reviewer has already read the argument.

One caution: the summary is where a weak appeal tries to compensate for thin evidence by asserting harder. Yours isn't thin — you have biopsy, dermoscopy, treatment history, and literature. So the summary should be calm and specific, not emphatic. "The record establishes X" beats "it is abundantly clear that X."

If you paste the full draft once it's revised, I'll check that the summary's claims actually match what the body supports — that's the most common place a good appeal overreaches.
